visible.summary: Niger is dangerous for trans visitors — and newly criminalising: in March 2025 the junta's Charter of Refoundation explicitly outlawed “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” for the first time (Article 25). Junta rule, jihadist insurgency, no recourse.
visible.tangentialFactors: The March 2025 charter explicitly criminalises “LGBTQIA+ practices” — trans visitors are named targets of the new provision.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: March 2025 criminalisation is brand new; enforcement undocumented.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview, last updated 12 March 2026: in March 2025 Niger explicitly outlawed same-sex acts for the first time — Article 25 of the junta's Charter of Refoundation bans 'LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior' during the five-year transition following the July 2023 coup. No specific penalties are set yet, but a 2023 draft penal code proposes up to five years for same-sex conduct, 20 years for conducting/officiating/witnessing a same-sex marriage and five years for participating in or financing 'homosexual' organisations. Earlier in 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency Article 276 (up to three years) and the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them; the code fixes age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts versus 13 for different-sex acts.

BBC News live page (December 2022): Niger's lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, moved by MP Nana Djibou Harouna of the southern Maradi region — weeks after a Maradi court acquitted two young women of lesbianism charges because no legislation criminalised same-sex relationships. Documents the legislative trail into the 2025 criminalisation.

The Guardian (1 July 2026): at least 40 people have been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men — including high-ranking military officials — imprisoned across Niger following the introduction of a new penal code earlier in 2026, in what campaigners describe as a 'witch-hunt' with a 'toxic' climate; sources also fear an HIV/AIDS resurgence as access to PrEP drugs collapses. Current enforcement evidence for the record.

Agence Nigérienne de Presse (state news agency, French): headline 'Le Niger criminalise la Pratique LGBTQIA+ dans le pays' — official state-press announcement of the criminalisation. Page body was largely navigation content at fetch time; headline finding only.

visible.summary: Chad is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct criminalised since 2017 (misdemeanour, up to 2 years); junta-adjacent governance; no LGR; no community infrastructure; very thin data.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised since 2017 (up to 2 years) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

sources.claim: US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report, Chad: criminalisation section states the law criminalised consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults with punishments ranging from three months to two years' imprisonment — official current-law baseline for visitor exposure; report also covers societal abuses.

US State Dept 2010 Human Rights Report, Chad (pre-criminalisation baseline): law prohibited but did not define 'unnatural acts' with no evidence it was used against LGBT persons that year; no known LGBT organisations and few reports of violence, most persons discreet due to social strictures — documents the pre-2017 legal climate.
US State Department 2006 Human Rights Report for Chad: documents the Deby regime's abuses - extrajudicial killings, torture, MINURCAT withdrawal - general context.

HuffPost/GroundTruth Project analysis: while further criminalisation attempts failed in Ethiopia and Rwanda, they succeeded in Chad and Nigeria — situates Chad's criminalisation drive within the broader wave of conservative anti-LGBT advocacy, relevant context for how the law's trajectory developed.

visible.summary: Gabon demands real caution — and on a surprising positive trajectory: after briefly criminalising same-sex intimacy in 2019, it decriminalised in 2020, and in November 2024 voters ratified a new constitution that rejected calls to criminalise homosexuality. No LGR; social conservatism; but the constitutional debate is now public and the pro-criminalisation side lost.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2020 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2024 constitution rejected criminalisation.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: 2020 decriminalisation + 2024 constitution are formal; social climate lags.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): criminalised same-sex intimacy in 2019 (max 6 months + US$8,561 fine), repealed in 2020 after Senate approval — reversal sharply divided public opinion; Nov-2024 constitution (military regime since Aug-2023) codifies privacy (Art.18) but retains Art.16 marriage definition; no legal gender recognition, LGBTI groups cannot register; same-sex relations legal for men and women per its country page (with caveat that criminalisation remains 'No' nationwide only since the 2020 repeal).

Erasing 76 Crimes (25 Nov 2024): Gabon's new constitution was ratified by referendum 16 Nov 2024 (over 90% yes, ~55% turnout) and rejected civil-society demands to re-criminalise homosexuality, adding LGBT+-protective privacy provisions — but codifies a marriage definition excluding same-sex couples. Context: Aug-2023 military coup ended 56 years of Bongo-family rule.

US State Department 2019 Human Rights Report for Gabon: official assessment covering the year the new penal code criminalised same-sex conduct - documents the legal change and societal discrimination.

LGBTQ Nation (13 Dec 2019): Gabon criminalised same-sex relations by law passed quietly in July 2019 — up to 6 months + 5m CFA francs (~US$8,500); two men already arrested and released only after paying police bribes; Gabon inherited no colonial-era sodomy law (independence 1960). Enforcement precedent: arrests occurred within months of enactment — later reversed by the 2020 repeal.
Washington Blade (July 2020): Gabon formally decriminalised homosexuality - the National Assembly overturned the 2019 ban, restoring the pre-2019 status where same-sex conduct was not criminal.

Gabon Review (29 Oct 2019, French): Law 042/2018 of 5 Jul 2019 (new penal code) criminalises same-sex relations without naming 'homosexuality' — Art.402 files 'les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe' under 'atteintes aux mœurs' (sexual assaults/attacks on morals); earlier Dec-2013 police arrest of two alleged 'gay marriers' released. Primary-source detail on the criminalisation year (2019) later reversed in 2020.

visible.summary: Burundi is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Same-sex conduct has been criminalised since 2009 (2 years), and the head of state himself has called for mob violence: in December 2023, President Ndayishimiye said LGBT people should be “taken to a stadium and stoned” because “that's what they deserve” — condemned by HRW as stoking fear; the Iteka League called it a call to lynching. There is no LGR, no community infrastructure (the oldest rights group works from exile), and arbitrary detention is routine.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised since 2009 — the vehicle by which trans people (legally their birth sex) are prosecuted; also a direct risk for trans visitors with partners.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Presidential incitement is documented by HRW (Jan 2024).

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Jan 2024): 'Burundi President Stokes Fear Among LGBT People' — President Ndayishimiye's call to 'stone' homosexuals; HRW urges the ruling party to renounce persecution.

SOS Médias Burundi (Jan 2024): after President Évariste Ndayishimiye called for 'homosexuals to be stoned', LGBTQ Burundians reported terror; the Iteka League (in exile) called the remarks 'a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people'. Members of two LGBTQ associations, speaking anonymously, described the remarks as 'a real license to kill (us)'. Same-sex relations are criminalised in Burundi.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Burundi: documents the country's crisis (extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention, media shutdowns) and includes the section on acts of violence and discrimination against LGBT persons - same-sex conduct criminalised since 2009, with arrests and harassment documented.
US State Department 2009 Human Rights Report for Burundi (archived): covers the year the penal code criminalised same-sex conduct; documents discrimination against gays and lesbians.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Burundi: lists discrimination against gays and lesbians among common human-rights abuses, alongside security-force killings, torture and harsh prison conditions.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Burundi: documents torture, extrajudicial executions, prolonged pretrial detention, and discrimination against LGBT persons under the criminalised framework.

visible.summary: Guinea is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (3 years); a 2024 UPR stakeholder report documents violence and discrimination from both state and non-state actors; junta rule since 2021; no LGR.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (3 years) — trans visitors captured via birth-sex status and partner risk.

sources.claim: The Advocates for Human Rights UPR stakeholder report on Guinea (Oct 2024): Guinea criminalises consensual same-sex relations while police commit arbitrary arrests, harassment and extortion that deepen stigma and fear; LGBTQ+ people live in a hostile, sometimes lethal environment with threats of physical violence and discrimination on orientation, gender-identity and expression grounds.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Guinea: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised (Article 325, 'indecency' provisions); documents violence and discrimination against LGBT persons and police harassment.

The Advocates for Human Rights + Khaleem Ali joint UPR stakeholder report (Oct 2024) on LGBT+ rights in Guinea: criminalisation of consensual same-sex activity; police arbitrary arrests, harassment and extortion; a hostile and 'sometimes deadly' environment; widespread stigmatisation hinders reporting of violence.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Guinea: documents security-force torture, prison abuse, FGM, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal discrimination.

Wikipedia, LGBTQ rights in Guinea (current): Article 274 of the 2016 Penal Code punishes same-sex conduct with six months to three years' imprisonment, a fine of GNF 500,000–1,000,000, or both; enforcement operates through arrests based on clothing and appearance, releases commonly bought by payment to police, and the law used as a basis for extortion; no legal gender recognition.

visible.summary: Liberia is dangerous for trans visitors. Sodomy is criminalised (1 year, both sexes — a domestic-origin law, never colonised); a legislator is seeking support for a harsh 2024 anti-homosexuality bill (so far unsuccessful); mob violence is documented; no LGR.
visible.tangentialFactors: Sodomy criminalised (1 year, both sexes) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2024 bill (not passed) signals trajectory.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Active hostile bill (2024) not yet passed.

sources.claim: Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Oct 2024): Rep. Johnson N. Williams is seeking lawmakers' support for a harsh anti-homosexuality bill filed that summer; related proposals would imprison children as young as 10 years old for gay sex — documents active legislative threat beyond the existing statute.

UNDP/OHCHR 'SOGIR in Africa: Liberia Country Report' (April 2020): participatory review and analysis of the legal, social and human-rights environment for people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity in Liberia.

NPR (9 Apr 2012, 'Liberian LGBT Rights Under Spotlight'): anti-gay sentiment growing since the US announced plans to promote LGBT rights overseas; new legislation proposed longer jail time for homosexuality and a group distributed fliers targeting gay-rights supporters.

The Guardian (19 Mar 2012, Monrovia): Nobel Peace Prize president Ellen Johnson Sirleaf defended laws criminalising homosexuality in a joint interview; her remarks drew international comment on Liberia's stance (Blair declined to comment).
